To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
elite powerlifters had significantly more fibres than controls but the fibres were significantly smaller.

elite powerlifters have a greater number of muscle fibes, but not greater muscle fibre size than trained controls, that the ultrastructural characteristics of the muscle of elite powerliftes and trained controls are very similar, but that elite powerliftes have more central nuclei and atrophic fibres than controls.

Muscle ultrastructure of a large group of elite powerliftes and bodybuilders was similar to that seen in a group of subjects who had undergone 6 month of heavy resistance training, except that there was a higher incidence of structural damage in the elite group.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of resistance training on muscle fibre size and ultrastructure in elite powerlifters, elite bodybuilders, and healthy volunteers.
the muscle ultrastructural characteristics of a group of elite powerlift and bodybuilders and the effects of 6 months of resistance training on muscle ultrastructure.
the ultrastructure of the skeletal muscle of elite powerliftes and bodybuilders, and the effects of heavy resistance training on the ultrastructure of skeletal muscle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the elite group of powerlifters and/or bodybuilders had an increased total number of fibres, a lower percentage of Type I fibres and a higher percentage of Type IIA fibres than the trained controls, and that the elite group had a lower mitochondrial volume density than the trained control group.
the muscle of elite powerlifts and bodybuilders is not different from that of a trained group of subjects in fibre size, type, or fibre type proportions.
elite powerlifters or bodybuilders have no significant differences in muscle fibre areas, fibre types or mitochondrial volume densities from a group of well-trained controls.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
elite powerlifters have a greater muscle mass than elite bodybuilders, but the muscle fibre characteristics of the two groups are similar.
despite large differences in muscle mass, the muscle fibre composition of elite bodybuilders and powerlifters is very similar to that of a group of trained controls.

the ultrastructural differences between elite and non-elite powerlifters and between elite and nonelite bodybuilders are not related to the differences in strength or muscle size, but rather are related to the differences of training experience, training volume, and the use of anabolics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
elite powerlifters or bodybuilders do not have a different muscle fiber composition than other people who train with weights.
muscle hypertrophy can be achieved with a relatively modest increase in fibre size.
the elite group did not differ from the control group with respect to fibre size or percentage distribution of fibre types.
